In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
aging per se in the ART-treated HIV-1 infected individual does not further impair memory B cell populations, and that the main effect is the HIV-1 infection.
the impact of aging on memory B cell populations is not as severe as previously thought and is not exacerbated in HIV-1 infected individuals.

the age-related changes in the B cell compartment of HIV-1-infected patients are not more severe than those observed in the HIV-2 population, and that the changes are mainly due to the HIV-1 infection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HIV-1 infection in ART-treated patients, regardless of age, impairs the memory B cell compartment.
the aging process does not worsen the impairments of memory B cells in HIV-1 infected individuals.
HIV-1 impairs memory B cells and aging does not worsen this impairment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the age of patients should not be considered as an exclusion criterion for HIV-1 vaccination trials.
the impaired memory B cells in HIV-1 infected individuals are restored to normal levels by long term ART therapy.
, in the context of HIV-1 infection and ART treatment, the age of patients does not impact on B cell subpopulation distribution and phenotype.
